title: Environments and CI/CD
summary: Why Notely runs in three places (local, preview, production), how each gets its own settings and data, and how automatic checks stop broken code before it deploys.
youWillLearn: The three environments and what each one is for
How environment variables let the same code talk to different databases
What CI runs on every pull request, and how a red check blocks a merge
Why production secrets must never reach preview builds

glossary.environment: One place your app runs, with its own settings and data: your laptop, a preview address, or the live site.
glossary.environment variable: A named setting given to the app from outside the code, like a database address or an API key.
glossary.preview deployment: A temporary copy of the app built from one branch, with its own web address, for checking before merging.
glossary.staging: A shared test environment set up like production but filled with fake data.
glossary.CI: Continuous integration: a robot that runs your checks (lint, types, tests) on every push.
glossary.CD: Continuous deployment: every merge to main is built and released automatically.
glossary.pipeline: The fixed sequence of steps code goes through from push to live: install, check, build, deploy.
glossary.required check: A CI job that must pass before GitHub lets anyone merge a pull request.
glossary.lint: An automatic read-through of the code that flags likely mistakes and style problems.

steps.title: Where Notely runs today
body: Notely's users reach the app server, the computer running Notely's live code. It keeps their notes in the database. Together, that live setup is called production.
Maya also runs Notely on her laptop, to try changes before they go live. A settings file on the laptop gives it the database address: the very same one the live app uses.

scene.caption: The live app and Maya's laptop both talk to the same database.

steps.title: One database for everything
body: Maya is building a delete all my notes button. On her laptop she clicks it a few times to try it.
Real users' notes disappear. Nothing was wrong with her laptop. It was talking to the one database that mattered.

callout.text: Rehearsing a play on the real stage, during the real show, in front of the paying audience.

changes: ~ Laptop: trying a delete-all-notes button
~ Database: real users' notes deleted
~ Tests touch real data, and it hurt

scene.caption: A test click on the laptop deletes real notes in the live database.

steps.title: Three places, three sets of data
body: The fix: run the same code in separate environments, each with its own data.

Local is the laptop, with a throwaway database. Preview is a copy of the app per branch, on test data. Production is the live app server and the only place with real users. A mistake in the first two costs nothing.
changes: − 5,000 users: out of frame for now
+ Local DB and Test DB: throwaway data for trying things
+ Preview: a copy of the app for each branch
~ Tests touch Real data → Test data

scene.caption: Three environments in three columns, each with its own database.

steps.title: Same code, different settings
body: How does one codebase know which database to use? Environment variables: named settings handed to the app from outside the code. The code reads SUPABASE_URL, and each environment fills in a different address.
On the laptop they live in .env.local, never committed. On Vercel you set them per environment.

code.caption: vercel env pull .env.local copies the Development values from Vercel to your laptop.

callout.text: In Next.js, Notely's toolkit, any variable starting with NEXT_PUBLIC_ is copied into the code every browser downloads. Only public values go there. Never the Claude API key or the Supabase service role key.

changes: ~ Each column's link: the address now comes from its own settings

scene.caption: Same code in every column; only the settings, and so the database, differ.

steps.title: A preview for every branch
body: Each pull request gets a preview deployment: a real build of that branch at its own web address. Send it to a client, test it on your phone, click every state.
Previews point at test data. That can be one shared staging database, or a fresh database copy per pull request if your Supabase plan offers branching.

callout.text: For client work, the preview link is your review tool. The client approves the new flow on the preview, then you merge. No "it looked different on my screen" surprises.

changes: ~ Laptop and App Server columns step back
~ Preview and Test DB in focus: one preview per pull request

scene.caption: The preview column: a real build of one branch, on test data.

steps.title: CI: a robot checks every push
body: Separate environments protect data. CI protects code. On every push to GitHub, a machine installs the app and runs the same checks: lint (an automatic read-through for likely mistakes), type check, tests.
Then CD takes over: merge to main, and production deploys on its own. The whole route from push to live is the pipeline.

callout.text: A preflight checklist. The pilot is experienced, and still runs the same list before every take-off, because forgetting one item once is enough.

changes: − Laptop, Local DB, Test DB, Database: we follow the code now
+ GitHub: stores the code and its pull requests
+ CI: a robot that runs checks on every push
~ Merge gate None → Warns

scene.caption: Every push goes through CI. A merge to main deploys production.

steps.title: The CI file, line by line
body: On GitHub, CI is a settings file in .github/workflows/. This one runs on every pull request and every push to main.
Each run line is a command you could type yourself. If one fails, the job turns red and the rest stop. Vercel builds and deploys separately, through its own GitHub connection.

code.code:
name: CI
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with: { node-version: lts/*, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npx tsc --noEmit
      - run: npm test
code.caption: npm ci installs exactly what the lockfile says, so CI matches your laptop.

callout.text: Ask Claude Code to add this file, then check: does every script it calls exist in package.json? Does it run on pull_request? Are secrets read from ${{ secrets.NAME }}, never pasted in? Push a deliberately broken commit once to see it turn red.

changes: ~ CI: install, lint, type check and tests, in that order

scene.caption: CI runs four commands on every push.

steps.title: Red check, locked door
body: A check that only warns gets ignored on busy days. Make it a required check: in GitHub's settings, add a rule on main that the CI job must pass.
Now a pull request with a failing test cannot be merged, not by you, a teammate, or Claude Code. Broken code stops before production, not after.
changes: ~ CI: one test fails
~ CI → App Server: the merge is blocked
~ Merge gate Warns → Blocks

scene.caption: A red check locks the door to production.

steps.title: Production secrets stay in production
body: A tempting shortcut: copy every production setting into Preview "so it works". Now every preview address, the ones you send to clients and testers, reads and writes real data with full-power keys.
Give Preview its own test database and its own API keys with low limits. If a preview leaks, nothing real is exposed.

callout.text: Vercel's Preview settings apply to every branch. A half-finished branch with a bug and a production service role key (a key that skips every access rule) is a data breach waiting for a link to be shared.

changes: − GitHub and CI
+ Test DB and Database: the two databases again
~ Preview → Database: copied production keys reach real data
~ Tests touch Test data → Real data

scene.caption: With production keys, a preview reaches the real database.

steps.title: Recap: separate places, automatic gates
body: Run the same code in three environments: local, preview, production. Environment variables point each one at its own data and keys, and only production touches real users.
CI runs the same checks on every push. Make them required, and a red check blocks the merge. Merging to main is then the only way to deploy.
changes: − Preview → Database link: Preview gets its own test keys
~ Test DB back in use
~ Tests touch Real data → Test data

scene.caption: Each environment talks only to its own database.

quiz.question: Maya wants to try a database change that drops a column. Where should she run it first?

options.text: On production, late at night when traffic is low.
options.why: Low traffic does not make a dropped column come back. Try destructive changes where data is fake.

options.text: Locally or on a preview database, then production after it works.
options.why: That is what non-production environments are for. A mistake there costs a reset, not real users' data.
Backups help you recover, but restoring is slow and loses recent changes. Prevention is far cheaper.

quiz.question: Claude Code added NEXT_PUBLIC_ANTHROPIC_API_KEY so the browser can call Claude directly. What is wrong?

options.text: Nothing, as long as the variable is set on Vercel and not committed.
options.why: Where it is stored does not matter. The NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix copies the value into the code every visitor downloads.

options.text: The name is too long for Vercel.
options.why: The name is fine. The prefix is the problem.

options.text: The key is shipped to every browser. Call Claude from the app server with a private variable.
options.why: Anyone can open the downloaded code and spend your credits. The key must stay on the server, behind your own API route.

quiz.question: Your CI runs tests on every pull request, but last week someone merged a pull request with a failing test anyway. What fixes this?

options.text: Make the CI job a required check on main.
options.why: A required check turns the result into a gate. GitHub will not allow a merge until the job passes.

options.text: Run the tests again after the merge.
options.why: That finds the bug after it is already on its way to production.

options.text: Ask everyone to look at the checks before merging.
options.why: Good intentions fail on busy days. A rule the machine enforces does not.

takeaways: Run the same code in three environments: local, preview, production. Only production touches real data.
Environment variables carry the differences. NEXT_PUBLIC_ values are public; secrets never get that prefix.
Every pull request gets a preview. Point it at test data, never at production keys.
CI runs lint, types and tests on every push. Make it a required check so red blocks the merge.
